reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Endocrine Society
clinicalPearls: A rare cause of spontaneous hypoglycaemia driven by autoantibodies to endogenous insulin in patients who have never received exogenous insulin
Characteristically causes postprandial or late fasting hypoglycaemia as antibody-bound insulin dissociates unpredictably from its carrier
The biochemical picture during hypoglycaemia shows very high insulin with detectable C-peptide and, crucially, positive insulin autoantibodies
Total measured insulin is often disproportionately elevated because antibody-bound insulin accumulates in the circulation
Strongly associated with particular HLA haplotypes and often triggered by sulfhydryl-containing drugs or other medications
It has a well-recognised association with other autoimmune disorders, notably Graves disease, and with certain plasma cell dyscrasias
Distinguishing it from insulinoma and factitious hypoglycaemia is essential and rests on the antibody status and insulin-to-C-peptide relationship
The condition is frequently self-limiting, and management focuses on removing precipitating drugs, dietary measures to blunt glycaemic swings, and immunosuppression in severe cases
reference.pathophysiology: Insulin autoimmune syndrome is caused by high-titre autoantibodies directed against endogenous insulin. After a meal, insulin is secreted normally and much of it binds to the circulating antibodies, blunting its immediate action; later, insulin dissociates from the antibodies in an uncoordinated fashion, delivering a bolus of free insulin at a time when it is no longer needed and provoking hypoglycaemia. This buffering-and-release mechanism produces the characteristic delayed postprandial or fasting hypoglycaemia. Genetic susceptibility is conferred by specific HLA class II alleles, and the autoantibody response is often precipitated by sulfhydryl-containing or other drugs, or arises in the context of coexisting autoimmune or plasma cell disorders.
additionalDifferentials: Factitious hypoglycaemia from surreptitious insulin or sulfonylurea use
Adrenal insufficiency and other endocrine causes of hypoglycaemia
Type B insulin resistance from insulin receptor antibodies
additionalInvestigations: Simultaneous glucose, insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin during a hypoglycaemic episode
Sulfonylurea screen to exclude factitious hypoglycaemia
Assessment of insulin-to-C-peptide relationship and consideration of assay interference
Imaging to exclude insulinoma when biochemistry is ambiguous
Screening for associated autoimmune disease and drug/medication review
redFlags: Severe or recurrent hypoglycaemia causing loss of consciousness, seizures, or neuroglycopenia requiring urgent glucose
Hypoglycaemia unawareness increasing the risk of dangerous episodes
Precipitating culprit drug that must be identified and withdrawn promptly
reference.prognosis: Many cases remit spontaneously over weeks to months, especially once a precipitating drug is stopped; dietary modification controls symptoms in most, and immunosuppression is effective for refractory disease, so the overall outlook is generally favourable.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing insulinoma and pursuing pancreatic surgery without checking insulin autoantibodies
Overlooking a precipitating sulfhydryl-containing or other drug
Misinterpreting very high insulin levels without recognising antibody interference in the assay
Failing to screen for coexisting autoimmune disease such as Graves disease
